safety_line: Bites are rare and defensive but medically significant — alpha-latrotoxin can cause serious symptoms. See a doctor for a suspected bite, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Glossy jet black body with a red hourglass mark on the underside of the abdomen
Messy, strong, low web in undisturbed corners — garages, meter boxes, woodpiles
Hides by day, hangs upside down at night
Females about 1.25 cm body length, males much smaller and rarely seen

look_alikes.difference: Black widow is glossy black with a red hourglass; brown widow is tan-brown with an orange hourglass and a spiky, sandspur-like egg sac.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the underside of the abdomen and any egg sac, from a few feet away.

copy.what_it_means: Bites are rare and almost always defensive — they happen when a hand reaches blind into her hiding spot. This is the one Florida spider worth professional attention when found where kids or pets play.
copy.fact: Bites are rare and defensive — nearly all happen when a hand reaches blind into her hiding spot.
copy.blurb: The one Florida spider worth professional attention when found where kids or pets play.

tech_notes: Confirm red hourglass underside. Deweb + void treatment in undisturbed harborage; advise on clutter/storage reduction.

safety_line: Venom is potent but this species injects less of it and bites less readily than the black widow. See a doctor for a suspected bite, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Tan to brown with an orange hourglass underneath (less bold than the black widow’s red)
Spiky, spherical egg sacs like tiny sea mines — the clearest tell
Web in furniture joints, meter boxes, and pool-cage corners
Tends to curl up rather than attack when disturbed

look_alikes.difference: Brown widow is tan-brown with an orange hourglass and a spiky egg sac; black widow is glossy black with a red hourglass and a smooth egg sac.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the underside of the abdomen and any egg sac, from a few feet away.

copy.what_it_means: Now more common than black widows in much of Florida, but notably shyer and less prone to bite. Respect rather than panic — gloves when moving stored patio furniture, and treatment if egg sacs multiply.
copy.fact: Now more common than black widows in much of Florida — but notably shyer and less prone to bite.
copy.blurb: Respect, don’t panic. Gloves when moving stored patio furniture; treat if egg sacs multiply.

tech_notes: Confirm orange hourglass + spiky egg sac. Deweb + void treatment; advise on clutter/storage reduction.

safety_line: Bites only if held or pinched, and feel about like a bee sting. No medical concern for most people.
traits: Large yellow-and-tan spider, females 24-40 mm, in a huge wheel web across paths
Web silk has a golden tint in sunlight
Brown-orange banded legs with tufts of hair on some segments
Sits head-down near the top of the web

look_alikes.difference: Golden silk orb-weaver has banded, tufted legs and a golden web; yellow garden spider has a bold black-and-yellow abdomen and a zigzag web decoration.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo of the whole web plus a close-up of the leg pattern.

copy.what_it_means: Eats mosquitoes and flies all day and rebuilds damaged sections of its web nightly. Relocate the web if it crosses a walkway; there is no need to kill the spider.
copy.fact: Her silk is, weight for weight, tougher than steel — and she rebuilds damaged sections of the web nightly.
copy.blurb: Eats mosquitoes and flies all day. Relocate the web if it’s across your walkway; don’t kill the engineer.

tech_notes: Beneficial; no treatment. If relocation is requested, move the whole web frame rather than destroying it.

safety_line: Not dangerous to people, though a bite from handling one can be locally painful. No medical concern for most people.
traits: Very large, flat body about 1 inch long with a 3-5 inch leg span
Legs angle forward like a crab, letting it squeeze into narrow gaps
Explosively fast when startled
Tan to brown with a cream marginal band around the carapace

look_alikes.difference: Huntsman spiders are flatter with crab-like forward legs; wolf spiders are stouter, hairier, and their eyes reflect flashlight light distinctly.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo of the leg posture from above, plus a flashlight eye-shine check at night.

copy.what_it_means: Terrifying-looking and not considered dangerous, but genuinely useful — it actively hunts and eats cockroaches. One on patrol is a roach’s worst night; there is no need to treat for it.
copy.fact: A dedicated cockroach hunter — one huntsman on patrol is a roach’s worst night.
copy.blurb: Terrifying-looking, not considered dangerous, genuinely useful. The scream is optional.

tech_notes: Beneficial predator of roaches; no treatment needed. Relocate outdoors if the customer prefers it gone.

safety_line: Venom is not dangerous to people; a bite from handling one can be locally painful, like a bee sting.
traits: No web — hunts on the ground at speed
Stout, hairy, brown to tan with at least one row of dark stripes from the eyes to the abdomen
Eyeshine sparkles distinctly when scanned with a flashlight at night
Females carry an egg sac, then dozens of spiderlings, on their back

look_alikes.difference: Wolf spiders are stouter and hairier with distinct flashlight eye-shine; huntsman spiders are flatter with crab-like forward-angled legs.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo of the leg posture from above, plus a flashlight eye-shine check at night.

copy.what_it_means: Mothers carry their spiderlings piggyback — dozens riding along until they can hunt on their own. This is free roach and cricket control; scoop-and-release beats squishing.
copy.fact: Mothers carry their spiderlings piggyback, dozens riding shotgun — one of the few spiders that does this.
copy.blurb: Free roach and cricket control. Scoop-and-release beats squishing.

tech_notes: Beneficial predator; indicates outdoor insect activity nearby. No treatment needed; check door sweeps if found indoors repeatedly.
